headline: Render an object identifier, match a header name and read a media type through operations a replacement cannot answer.
summary: A method reached through an index is the same replaceable operation as one reached through a call: `rows[i].toString()` reads `toString` off whatever that element is, exactly as `f(x).toString()` reads it off a call result. Thirty-three such reads were still live across thirteen modules, and the ones that matter are not the registry tables built when a module loads but the values other decisions are made from: the dotted string an object identifier is rendered to, which every algorithm and extension decision in this toolkit is made on; the header name a response value is selected under; the media type that decides which parser a body is handed to; and the content-type parameter that says where a multipart response is split. Each now reads through an operation bound when its module loaded.

Fixed: An object identifier is rendered to its dotted form through operations bound when the module loaded, and its arcs are collected by defining each index rather than by appending to the array. Three different replacements each decided that string, which is the value `pki.oid` resolves, which selects a signature algorithm and which names an extension: a replaced integer conversion made the content octets of `1.2.3` render as `1.3.4`, and an accessor inherited at the first index of every array took each arc as it was collected and made the same octets render as `0.1.3`. Appending stores at an index, and a store consults the prototype chain for a setter, so a list this build assembles is now built by defining its indexes.

A media type is read on the delimiter character and folded through a captured conversion, in `pki.acme`, `pki.cmp` and `pki.ct`. The token decides which parser a response body is handed to, and it was produced by splitting, trimming and folding through live operations. Splitting is now a character scan, which this toolkit requires in its libraries because a separator's own split hook is part of that operation.

`pki.est` reads a content-type parameter through captured operations, and collects the segments it searches by defining each index. That is where the RFC 7030 multipart boundary comes from, so the value decides where a multi-part response is divided: measured, a header declaring `boundary=wire` yielded `forged`, both through a replaced append and through an accessor inherited at an array index. The name comparison that selects a parameter, the slicing that extracts it and the quote stripping around it were each live, as were the name and value of every header on a part, which is where a part's own content type comes from: measured, a part declaring `application/pkcs8` was read as `application/pkcs7-mime` carrying `smime-type=certs-only`. Its two case-insensitive header lookups are folded through the capture on both sides of the comparison.

`pki.acme` parses a Link header through captured operations: the header is divided into links, each link into parameters, and the target cut out of its angle brackets, all through operations bound when the module loaded. The relation decides whether a header names a resource the client will follow and the target is the URL it would fetch, and both were produced by methods read off the live prototype: measured, a header stating one alternate chain resolved to a different URL.

`pki.cmc.build` selects which request arm a message carries through a selection that reads each candidate once and builds its own result, rather than through a method that is both read off the prototype and specified to construct its result through a replaceable protocol.

The algorithm, extension and criticality tables that `pki.path.validate`, `pki.cms`, `pki.crl`, `pki.key`, `pki.webcrypto`, `pki.x509` and the signature-scheme registry build when they load are built through captured walks, so a replacement installed before a module loads cannot decide which rows exist.
Changed: The check that holds these modules to captured operations now counts a method reached through an index, not only one reached through a call. It is the same receiver one bracket over, and the earlier form could not see it: two live copies in the RFC 5280 policy-mapping walk, where the copy becomes a node's expected policy set, were found by other means.
